name: Dengue Fever

pathogens.why: The combination of fever, retro-orbital pain, myalgia/arthralgia, rash, and thrombocytopenia in an Aedes-endemic area (essentially all of urban and semi-urban India in season) is classic for dengue; serology/antigen testing confirms the diagnosis.

investigations.why: Detects dengue viral antigen early in illness before antibody response develops.
Confirms diagnosis when NS1 is negative or testing occurs later in the course; IgG pattern can also suggest primary vs. secondary infection.
Tracks thrombocytopenia and hematocrit trends, central to monitoring for plasma leakage and bleeding risk.
A rising hematocrit with falling platelets signals plasma leakage and impending severe dengue — the single most important trend to follow.
Transaminitis is common in dengue and severe elevation can indicate more severe disease.

references: National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme (NVBDCP) India Guidelines
reason: , and thrombocytopenia is consistent with dengue fever — a viral infection transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes. Antibiotics have no role. Management is supportive (careful fluid management, platelet/hematocrit monitoring) with vigilance for warning signs of progression to dengue with warning signs or severe dengue (plasma leakage, shock, bleeding, organ impairment).

clinicalPearls: Symptomatic dengue evolves through three phases: febrile, critical (plasma leakage), and recovery; most patients never enter the critical phase, but the possibility must be actively considered in every case (p.1714).

The critical/plasma-leakage phase characteristically begins around the time fever subsides (defervescence, roughly days 3-5), so worsening at this transition - not at peak fever - signals deterioration (p.1721).
A 'saddle-back' fever pattern (recurrence of fever after defervescence and a brief remission) can occur in a subset of patients (p.1714).
Most primary DENV infections are subclinical, and only about 25% of the ~400 million annual infections cause clinical illness (p.1711).
A positive tourniquet test (>=10 new petechiae per square inch on the upper arm after BP-cuff inflation for 5 min) reflects microvascular damage and is more often linked to severe dengue (p.1714).
Near defervescence a maculopapular rash typically starts on the trunk and spreads to the extremities and face; a separate transient macular rash may appear at illness onset (p.1714).
During recovery a patchy erythematous pruritic rash that desquamates may develop as extravascular fluid and effusions are reabsorbed (p.1722).
Early IgG appearing about 4 days after onset and rising rapidly suggests a secondary (rather than primary) infection, where IgG otherwise appears later and at much lower titers (p.1721).
harrison.pathophysiology: Dengue is caused by the four flavivirus (orthoflavivirus) serotypes DENV-1 to DENV-4, transmitted mainly by Aedes aegypti (and the secondary vector Aedes albopictus), which bite during the day. After infection of one serotype, the cross-protection against a different (heterotypic) serotype is only transient and wanes within weeks to a few weeks of convalescence; subsequent heterotypic infection can produce classic dengue or, less often, severe dengue. The progression to severe disease centers on immune-mediated enhancement, in which enhancing, non-neutralizing antibodies are implicated, whereas neutralizing antibodies are associated with lower viremia on reinfection. The hallmark of severe dengue is a vascular-leak syndrome producing increased capillary permeability, intravascular volume depletion, hypoalbuminemia, and serosal (pleural, ascitic) effusions; recent evidence assigns the DENV NS1 protein a key role in this vascular leak. Host/viral risk modifiers include age (susceptibility to severe dengue drops markedly after 12 years), the specific sequence and timing of serotype infections (e.g., DENV-1 then DENV-2 tends to be more severe), and viral-variant heterogeneity (p.1711, 1721).
additionalDifferentials: Zika virus disease (often misdiagnosed as dengue; low-grade fever, itchy maculopapular rash, arthralgia/myalgia, nonpurulent conjunctivitis)
Other arboviral fevers presenting as fever-and-myalgia syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Antigen-detection ELISA or RT-PCR (nucleic acid amplification) during the acute phase, useful within roughly the first 5 days of illness (p.1714, 1721)
Combination point-of-care testing pairing NS1 antigen with IgM antibody assay, increasingly used clinically (p.1721)
Paired (acute and convalescent) serology during recovery (p.1714)
Serum AST (often modestly elevated without true hepatic synthetic dysfunction) (p.1714)
Tourniquet test as a bedside marker of microvascular fragility (p.1714)
redFlags: Onset of restlessness or lethargy together with thrombocytopenia (<100,000/uL) and hemoconcentration 2-5 days into illness, typically at defervescence (p.1721)
Signs of plasma leakage: rising hematocrit/hemoconcentration, hypoalbuminemia, and serosal effusions (pleural effusion, ascites) (p.1721)
Circulatory compromise with narrowed pulse pressure, hepatomegaly, and cyanosis progressing to shock (p.1721)
Severe or spontaneous bleeding in the absence of a predisposing lesion (p.1721)
Severe organ dysfunction: altered mental status or seizures (CNS), arrhythmias (cardiac), acute kidney injury (renal), hepatic injury (p.1721)
harrison.prognosis: Most patients with uncomplicated dengue recover from the acute illness within 7-10 days, though convalescence may be prolonged and post-acute fatigue and depression are recognized sequelae. Among the millions of annual DENV infections, about 500,000 progress to severe dengue, with an overall case-fatality rate near 2.5%; with early recognition and good supportive care most patients with severe dengue respond well, and CFR at experienced tropical centers can be as low as ~1% (p.1714, 1721-1722).
pitfalls: Anchoring on the febrile phase and missing the critical phase, which paradoxically begins as fever declines rather than at its peak (p.1721).
Serologic cross-reactivity with antigenically similar orthoflaviviruses (yellow fever, Zika, Japanese encephalitis virus) - including after vaccination - can confound serologic diagnosis (p.1721).
Relying on antigen/nucleic-acid tests outside their acute-phase window: after about day 5 diagnosis must shift to serology (p.1721).
Failing to distinguish secondary from primary infection: early, rapidly rising IgG points to secondary infection and higher severe-disease risk (p.1721).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison endorses the WHO pragmatic categories that replaced the older 'dengue fever / dengue hemorrhagic fever / dengue shock syndrome' terminology: dengue without warning signs, dengue with warning signs (which directs inpatient management), and severe dengue. Severe dengue is defined as confirmed or presumptive dengue plus at least one of: (1) plasma leakage severe enough to cause shock or respiratory distress, (2) severe bleeding, or (3) severe organ dysfunction. Every patient with presumptive dengue of any severity should be assessed up front for warning signs and for the criteria of severe dengue, with the provisional diagnosis of severe dengue made clinically (p.1704, 1721).
